processing: Raw pu-erh handling: pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then sold loose or pressed, with no ripening pile.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as usual across Yiwu.
appearance_dry: Neat leaf with visible white down, usually pressed into a cake.
appearance_wet: Supple olive-green leaves, typical of large-leaf raw tea.
taste_profile: Full and smooth with a strong, mellow honey aroma, more refined and gentle than forceful.

brewing.notes: Short steeps in near-boiling water keep the honey aroma clean. A thin porcelain gaiwan suits a gentle tea like this.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year as raw pu-erh usually is, with spring lots most valued. Village-named cakes are mostly recent vintages, to be drunk young for the aroma or stored for years.
description:
Zhangjiawan is one of the seven villages in Yiwu's "seven villages, eight hamlets" grouping. What sets it apart is its past as much as its tea: it was a stop on the caravan route south from the northern tea mountains.

Processing is the normal raw pu-erh route, so the character comes from the place and its trees. The leaf is described as neat and downy, brewing to a golden liquor.

In the cup it is full and smooth with a strong honey aroma, and has been likened to a well-bred, quiet young lady rather than a showpiece. It suits short steeps, and the gentleness is the point, so do not push it for strength.

Ask for the year and season, and check the village is really the Yiwu one: Zhangjiawan is a common place name in China.
history: Zhangjiawan appears often in accounts of pu-erh's past. Before the war against Japan, merchants heading from the northern part of the Six Great Tea Mountains towards Lai Chau in Vietnam passed through it, and caravans rested there. That location helped make the name known early, though dates for its gardens are not recorded.
